description:
Hi! I’m Muthukumaran, a third-year Computer Science student at Chennai Institute of Technology and an OpenAI Student Collective Campus Lead. I enjoy building interactive web apps with React and Python, and I’ve built and demoed AI projects at hackathons.

For NASA Space Apps, I’m building Moonbase Blackout, a short game where students run a lunar outpost. When the power drops, can you keep life support running, grow enough food, and prepare for a solar storm? I want to make those trade-offs fun!
summary:
A solar storm is approaching, three astronauts are outside, and 12 battery units have to keep a lunar outpost alive. Moonbase Blackout puts students ages 7–12 in Mission Control. In Flight Recorder, they predict an outcome, rewind, and test a different decision. In one run, keeping the grow lights on leaves five rations and too little power to restart. In the replay, saving power restores the base, with two rations left.

The Mars dust-storm mission tests a different constraint: players must commit while their message to Earth is still in transit. An archived NASA solar alert, lunar terrain imagery, and a measured NASA/JPL radio light time ground the missions. By predicting an outcome and replaying a decision, students learn to explain how choices about life support, radiation shielding, food, and power affect crew safety and whether a base can recover. The game runs in a desktop or mobile browser without an account or download.
details:
The solar array is down. Three astronauts are outside, a solar storm is approaching, and Mission Control has 12 battery units. What do you keep running, and will you have enough power to restart the base?

Space Cursor AI built Moonbase Blackout for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players aged 7–12 take charge of a lunar outpost, then face a different power emergency on Mars. Both missions run in the browser on desktop and mobile without an account or download.

Play the Moon and Mars in 3D

Walk to the solar array on the Moon and repair it to recover power. On Mars, cross the outpost’s safe-zone boundary during a regional dust storm and secure exposed equipment while monitoring suit oxygen.

Play the Moon and Mars campaigns

Watch the three-minute walkthrough

Moon mission - Get the crew inside

Route emergency power to life support and the shelter. Watch the astronauts cross the map until the shelter counter reaches 3/3. Then decide whether to keep everyone shielded or send Ellis outside to repair the array. The repair can recover power at the cost of radiation exposure. The map, crew radio, and resource readings show what happens as the drill unfolds.

Mission Control confirms that all three astronauts have reached shelter.

Moon surface campaign. The solar array repair is complete, and the next field task appears.

Flight Recorder - Change one decision and replay

Students predict how a choice will affect the crew’s supplies, then rewind and test it. In the full blackout drill, the starting supplies and shelter plan are the same in both runs.

• Grow lights on. The crew has 5 rations and 4 battery units before restart. The base stays on emergency power.

• Grow lights off. The crew has 2 rations and 7 battery units before restart. The base comes back online.

Both runs keep the crew safe. A restart costs 6 battery units.

To reproduce the result, power life support and the grow lights, choose Wait in shelter, then Stay on reserves. In the debrief, select Rewind blackout. Repeat the shelter plan with the grow lights off, then select Restart the base.

Mars mission - Decide before Earth can answer

A dust storm cuts solar output. Students send a request to Earth, then choose whether to power the greenhouse or use stored food to save battery. They commit at 8:00 on the simulated mission clock. The request reaches Earth at 11:22, and the reply reaches Mars at 22:44. The event report shows the cost of their choice.

Mars surface campaign. The first equipment unit is secure, and the HUD shows the suit oxygen and safe-zone warning.

How NASA data shapes the missions

The January 3, 2024 GOES particle alert in NASA DONKI anchors the lunar storm scenario. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter south-pole mosaic supplies the Mission Control terrain. Opportunity’s observations inform the Mars dust-storm power loss, and Perseverance’s landing-day radio light time sets the Mars relay delay. Battery budgets, food costs, exposure points, and countdowns are simplified for training.

What students practice

Before a replay, ask, “If we save power now, what will the crew give up?” Students can predict the answer, test it, and use the debrief to explain why the outcome changed. The same exercise works for independent play or a classroom discussion.

What Space Cursor AI Built and How It Stands Out

We built the lunar Mission Control console and its mission rules, Flight Recorder, the Mars power and relay scenario, and the mobile controls.

  • Change one choice and replay. Students make a prediction, replay with the same starting supplies and shelter plan, and compare food, battery reserve, and restart status in a side-by-side debrief.
  • See crew safety change in real time. The shelter counter updates as each astronaut arrives. Sending Ellis out for a solar-array repair can recover power while increasing radiation exposure.
  • Make a decision before Earth can answer. On Mars, players commit to a power plan at 8:00, before their request reaches Earth at 11:22. The delay uses NASA/JPL’s Perseverance landing-day radio light time.

Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, JavaScript, and Three.js. Hosted on Vercel.

NOVA is an optional in-game assistant that uses current mission readings to explain the next task, suit oxygen, and base power, with a built-in guide if Cloudflare Workers AI is unavailable.

Project presentation

The slide deck summarizes the mission, Flight Recorder, and the NASA data behind the gameplay.
